key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the chain of circumstances leading to the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of rape, murder, and concealing the dead body of the victim child, supported by medical and scientific evidence, as well as the testimony of the child witness.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the child witness's testimony as categorical and credible, even though her comprehension of time and hours appeared lacking in maturity, which is considered unrealistic for a ten-year-old child from a rural background.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant failed to satisfactorily explain his whereabouts since he was last seen with the deceased and his knowledge of the location of the dead body, which is a strong link in the chain of circumstances against him.
trial_duration: Trial court and High Court concurrently recorded findings; conviction upheld; Supreme Court affirmed conviction
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court not specified
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: conviction upheld; High Court: conviction upheld; Supreme Court: partly allowed, death sentence commuted to life imprisonment
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant enticed a seven-year-old girl to accompany him on the pretext of picking lychee fruits, then committed rape on her, killed her, and dumped her body in bushes near the riverbank. The trial court and High Court found the prosecution successfully established a chain of circumstances leading to the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of rape, murder, and concealing the dead body.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant failed to discharge the burden cast upon him by Section 106 of the Evidence Act and could not satisfactorily explain his whereabouts after he was last seen with the deceased or his knowledge of the location of the dead body. They also highlighted the appellant's lack of criminal antecedents, poor socio-economic background, and unblemished jail conduct as mitigating factors.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the 'rarest of rare' test, balancing the crime test and criminal test, and considered the societal impact of the crime while weighing aggravating and mitigating factors.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Union of India v. V. Sriharan Alias Murugan and Ors., Dhananjoy Chatterjee, Laxman Naik, Kamta Tiwari
sentencing_rationale: The heinous nature of the crime, including brutal rape and murder of a seven-year-old girl, disclosed aggravating circumstances. However, the court considered the appellant's lack of criminal antecedents, poor socio-economic background, and unblemished jail conduct as mitigating factors, leading to a life sentence with a minimum of 30 years of actual imprisonment.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant had no criminal antecedents, came from a poor socio-economic background, had a family comprising of wife, children, and an aged father, and had unblemished jail conduct.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The heinous nature of the crime, including brutal rape and murder of a seven-year-old girl, which shocked the conscience and caused societal abhorrence.
other_sentence_order: The death sentence for the offence under Section 302 IPC was commuted into life imprisonment with a stipulation that the appellant shall not be entitled to premature release or remission before undergoing actual imprisonment for a period of 30 years. The direction for payment of half of the amount of fine to the mother of the deceased girl is also confirmed.
